description:
SPACE SHIELD | HUMANITY IN ORBIT

We are a team of innovators working to make human space exploration safer, smarter and healthier. At NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are exploring AI, 3D digital twins, and immersive technology to transform astronaut health monitoring. Our vision is to help space travelers understand changes in their physical and cognitive performance and make informed decisions during long missions, even far from Earth. Protecting explorers is essential to exploring farther.
summary:
Space Shield is a health monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration missions. On a journey to Mars, a medical team may be minutes away by radio and months away by ship, so crew members need to understand their own health without waiting for guidance from Earth. Space Shield puts two things they need most in one place: a clear view of radiation exposure and a quick daily record of how their body and mind are holding up.

The radiation module shows dose rates over 7, 14, or 30 days, with cumulative exposure, historical readings, and space-weather events such as coronal mass ejections. The daily check-in takes under a minute: heart rate and temperature, sleep and rest, and how the astronaut is feeling. Over time, these entries build a personal baseline, so the crew can spot changes against their own normal rather than a generic standard.
details:
The problem

Deep-space travel combines hazards that are rarely found together: space radiation, altered gravity, isolation, confinement, and disrupted sleep. Communication delays of up to 20 minutes each way mean crews can’t count on real-time medical support. Awareness of slow, cumulative changes, such as rising radiation dose or a gradual decline in sleep and mood, has to come from the crew itself.

What Space Shield does

Mission Dashboard
One screen shows mission day , communication delay , a radiation summary , and the most recent crew check in with direct access to both main modules.

Radiation monitor

Selectable 7-, 14-, and 30-day views show the latest dose rate, the period average, the peak reading, and estimated cumulative exposure. An interactive trend graph and a log of dated readings with their sources let astronauts see patterns, while space-weather event information explains why a spike may have occurred.

Daily crew check-in

A three-step flow keeps the habit light:

Heart rate and body temperature
Sleep and recovery
Emotional and psychological well-being

Health trends

Check-ins are stored as a running record and compared against the individual’s usual values, making unusual changes easier to notice early.

Guidance and sources

Each indicator comes with a plain-language explanation, so crew members without medical training understand what they are looking at and why it matters.

Design approach

The interface is dark-themed, which suits low-light spacecraft environments, and organized into separate modules, so a crew member can find what they need quickly. Charts and summaries are meant to be read at a glance, and the language avoids unnecessary clinical jargon.

How it responds to the NASA challenge

The challenge asks for software that supports astronaut health on space missions. Space Shield treats radiation exposure and personal health as connected parts of the same picture rather than separate tools. It also encourages regular check-ins in place of occasional assessments, so changes show up gradually in the data instead of surfacing only when something is already wrong.

Future development

• Integration with wearable sensors for automatic vital-sign capture
• Connection to spacecraft radiation and environmental systems
• Deeper analytics to flag meaningful deviations from baseline
• A channel for sharing records with medical teams on Earth

Prototype note

This version is a demonstration prototype. Radiation readings and mission data are sample values, not live spacecraft measurements. Health entries are entered by the user or loaded as demo data. Space Shield does not measure vital signs automatically or provide medical diagnosis, and it is a health-awareness concept rather than a replacement for professional medical assessment or mission-approved procedures.
